work: Yekl: A Tale of the New York Ghetto
creator: Abraham Cahan
notes: Mamie, the dance-hall girl Jake Podkovnik takes up with, boards in a Chrystie Street tenement; no house number is given. Jake and Gitl's own three rooms, in a new tenement, get no street. The east side of Chrystie between Canal and Houston was razed in the 1930s for Sara D. Roosevelt Park, so the building may not survive.
source_quote: Jake did start, mechanically, in the direction of Chrystie Street, where Mamie lodged.
source2_quote: near the house where she _boards_, on Chrystie Street

creator: Ayn Rand
address_as_given: the ghettoes of New York (Hell's Kitchen)
notes: Wynand's childhood home, before he builds his newspaper empire; the novel gives no street. Setting years are an estimate from his age in the novel's 1920s-30s present.
source_quote: Gail Wynand is a wealthy newspaper mogul who rose from a destitute childhood in the ghettoes of New York (Hell's Kitchen) to control much of the city's print media.

creator: Vera Caspary
address_as_given: Laura Hunt's apartment on East 62nd Street
notes: The apartment, the novel's crime scene, is described on page 35 in Waldo Lydecker's voice; it has a bay window on East 62nd Street. No house number or cross street was found, so the point sits mid-street near Lexington Avenue. Serialized in 1942 as Ring Twice for Laura; setting years are an estimate.
source_quote: the description (Page 35) of Laura Hunt’s apartment on East 62nd Street as given in the voice of newspaper columnist Waldo Lydecker
source2_quote: “I stood beside him in the bay window of Laura’s living room. East 62nd Street had yielded to the spirit of carnival…”

creator: Gerald Green
notes: Abelman, an aging general practitioner modeled on Green's father, lives and practices in Brownsville; he turns down the new house a television show offers him. The source calls the setting the late 1950s, but the novel came out in 1956, so the years here are the mid-1950s.
source_quote: The story takes place in the late 1950s in the Brownsville section of Brooklyn.

household: the Coney Island Dominators: Papa Arnold, Hector, Lunkface, Bimbo, Hinton, Dewey, Junior
creator: Sol Yurick
address_as_given: Coney Island, the Dominators' home turf
notes: The gang's home turf, where the survivors get back to at daybreak after the night's trek from the Bronx; no street or project is named in the source. Setting year is the novel's contemporary present.
source_quote: Among the gangs are the Coney Island Dominators, an African American / Hispanic gang who are the central characters of the novel.
source2_quote: Hinton, Dewey, and Junior finally arrive in Coney Island just before daybreak.

creator: Mario Puzo
notes: The family lives in a walk-up tenement flat in Hell's Kitchen; the source names no street, so the point is the neighborhood's center. The story runs from the late 1920s to the eve of Pearl Harbor.
source_quote: one family of New York City immigrants living in Hell’s Kitchen. Fresh from the farms in Italy, Lucia Santa struggles to hold her family together in a strange land.

creator: Harry Harrison
notes: On the run from the police in the novel's overcrowded 1999, Billy breaks into the derelict Navy Yard and lives there with Peter, who awaits the millennium. The yard is a large site, hence the radius.
source_quote: To evade capture, Billy leaves the city, eventually breaking into the abandoned Brooklyn Navy Yard, where he comes to live with Peter

creator: James Baldwin
notes: Tish (Clementine Rivers) lives with her family in Harlem while Fonny is jailed; the two grew up in the same neighborhood. The source gives no street.

creator: Judith Rossner
notes: Theresa grows up in the Bronx and later lives alone on the Upper West Side, where she is killed. The novel fictionalizes the 1973 murder of the teacher Roseann Quinn on the Upper West Side; the real building is not used here.
source_quote: Back in Theresa’s Upper West Side apartment, Gary is offended when, after sex, Theresa tells him to leave.
source2_quote: Five years ago, a young kindergarten teacher was murdered in her apartment on Manhattan’s Upper West Side.

creator: Akimi Yoshida
notes: From the side story Garden of Light (1994), set seven years after the main series; Eiji, now a photographer, has settled in the Village. The main series' mid-1980s apartments are not placed here.
source_quote: The story follows Akira Ibe, the niece of Shunichi Ibe, as she visits New York City and stays with Eiji, now an accomplished photographer living in Greenwich Village.

creator: Paul Auster

notes: Black writes in his apartment on Orange Street while Blue watches from across the street. No house number is given; the point is mid-street near Hicks Street.

source2_quote: Black, who spends nearly all his time writing (the story we're reading, perhaps?) in a Brooklyn Heights apartment.

creator: Paul Auster
notes: After a year in a Columbia dorm, Marco rents a fifth-floor studio in an elevator building on West 112th Street and furnishes it with his uncle's boxes of books. No number is given; the point is near Broadway. Source is a reader's chapter-by-chapter notes on the novel.
source_quote: He had lived in a collage dormitory for the first nine months, then he lived in an apartment West 112th street for three years.
source2_quote: Marco distinguishes himself in college with his bohemian lifestyle and moves into an apartment near the campus.

creator: Paul Auster
notes: Evicted and broke in the summer of 1969, Marco sleeps rough in Central Park, ending up sick in a cave there before Kitty Wu and Zimmer find him. The novel does not fix one spot.
source_quote: Central Park becomes Marco's new home. Here he seeks shelter from the pressure of the Manhattan streets.
source2_quote: He goes to live in Central Park. He gets sick, holes up in a cave

notes: Marco and Kitty rent a loft with Effing's parting gift of $7,000 after his death in 1970. No number is given; East Broadway runs from Chatham Square to Grand Street.

source2_quote: they use Effing’s parting gift of $7,000 to rent their own apartment.

work: Our House in the Last World
creator: Oscar Hijuelos
address_as_given: small, modest apartment ... in raucous Spanish Harlem
notes: Sources disagree: the publisher's description puts the family in Spanish Harlem, while an EBSCO study guide calls it an Upper West Side apartment building (see santinio-upper-west-side). Hijuelos himself grew up in Morningside Heights, and the novel is autobiographical.
source_quote: The fraught family of four shares their small, modest apartment with extended relatives in raucous Spanish Harlem.

work: Our House in the Last World
creator: Oscar Hijuelos

notes: The alternative placement to santinio-spanish-harlem; the point leans north toward Morningside Heights, where Hijuelos grew up. Treat the two records as one disputed home.
